newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Invasion of bikers brings fear to San Francisco.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Invasion of bikers brings fear to San Francisco.

text.p: Like a scene from the 1954 movie classic "The Wild One," an invasion of bikers has brought fear to San Francisco, outraged motorists, slowed traffic to a crawl and put police and politicians on the spot.

But the men and women who briefly took over city streets last week were not leather-clad Hell's Angels astride Harley-Davidsons. They wore shorts and T-shirts and rode bicycles -- and they promise to return in August.

An estimated 6,000 cyclists fanned out through downtown streets during the rush hour in an impressive display of pedal power. They were taking part in the monthly ride through the city called "Critical Mass," which is intended to promote bicycles as an alternative to cars.

But this ride was different. Ignoring an agreement that city officials believed they had with the cyclists to stick to an agreed route, groups of riders split off in all directions, reducing the city to chaos.

Hordes of cyclists took over streets, creating traffic gridlock and enraging motorists who honked their horns and fumed over missed flights and appointments. Motorists and cyclists engaged in angry shouting matches and fistfights as each accused the other of spitting or swerving toward them.

At some intersections, motorists got out of their cars and linked arms to stop the bicycles from getting through. Police turned out in force, arresting about 250 cyclists for disrupting traffic or running red lights and a few for assault. Two police officers were injured.
'CRITICAL MESS'

P.J. Johnston, a spokesman for Mayor Willie Brown, said the event, dubbed a "critical mess" by local media, "flew in the face of all the best intentions of the city and the police department" and could set back efforts by bicycle advocates to get cycle paths and other cycling facilities in the city.

"The vast majority of San Franciscans are so angry about what happened that it was really counter-productive to people who want to make San Francisco a bicycle-friendly place," he said, blaming the chaos on "a dedicated group of saboteurs."
Johnston said Brown would meet with police and others to decide the city's next step. "Critical Mass" is held on the last Friday of each month so the next would be on Aug. 29.
"The city is not going to allow a mob scene to occur every month ... Anarchy will not be allowed to reign on the streets of San Francisco," Johnston said.

At the best of times, there is little love lost between cyclists and motorists in this city of steep hills. Cyclists, particularly the hundreds of bicycle messengers who speed around San Francisco, complain that their lives are often endangered by reckless drivers. But other road users complain that cyclists often run red lights and ignore traffic laws.

Cyclists have held "Critical Mass" rides here since 1992, usually agreeing on a route just before setting out. Several other cities around the world have similar events. But many of the bicycle messengers who started the event now turn up their noses at it, saying it has been taken over by yuppies from the suburbs who rarely ride bicycles.

Last week's chaos was a slap at Brown, who called for a crackdown on "Critical Mass" after the June ride caused traffic gridlock. Later he backed away from the threat and city officials held talks with leaders of bicycling groups and compromised on an approved route with the usual police escort.
HARDLINE RIDERS SEE BETRAYAL

But hardline riders saw the agreement with the city as a betrayal of the freewheeling spirit of the ride. As cyclists gathered to begin the July ride, alternative route plans were circulated and groups set off in different directions. The advance publicity insured a huge turnout.
Bicycle messenger Daniel Thompson said the outcome was inevitable. "When the mayor decided to kind of challenge the ride, it changed. It became a confrontational thing," he said.

Participants in the "Critical Mass" rides say the movement has no leaders. "It's a really weird kind of group where everybody knows where to show up and doesn't want anybody telling them that's where they should show up," Thompson said.

Another messenger, Abdul Mubdi Abdullah Muhammad, placed a lot of the blame for last week's event on the media, which he said gave negative coverage to the ride. "The police I think were out of hand. Heads were bashed long before one person ever got on their bike and rode away," he said.

San Francisco police spokesman Sherman Ackerson said a small group of cyclists set out with the intention that they were "going to make a statement, were going to be uncivil." Now he said the city had to decide whether it would allow next month's "Critical Mass" to take place.
It could seek a court injunction to stop it, but Ackerson said it might be difficult to enforce. Meanwhile, the cyclists predict another big turnout.
